Empirical Research Plan: “CEO Pay, Firm Size, and the Market for Top Executives, 1970–2003”

------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen design: Two–Stage Least Squares (Instrumental Variables).

Why IV?  
• The central causal parameter of interest is the elasticity of CEO compensation with respect to firm size (market capitalization).  
• Firm size is endogenous: it is jointly determined with CEO quality, effort, and compensation policies, and is mechanically correlated with firm‐specific stock returns that may themselves be driven by the CEO.  
• We exploit plausibly exogenous, industry-wide valuation shocks that move a firm’s market cap for reasons that are largely outside the control of the focal CEO. A Bartik/shift–share style instrument delivers strong first‐stage power while retaining substantial cross-sectional and inter-temporal variation.

Design in one sentence:  Use the interaction of a firm’s pre-determined 1970 industry share with contemporaneous industry-level capitalization shocks to instrument for its own market capitalization and estimate the causal effect of firm size on CEO pay.

------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------------
Because the treatment is continuous (firm size), we describe the components of the IV design, not a binary treated/untreated grouping.

• Endogenous “treatment” variable  
  SIZE_it  = ln(market capitalization) of firm i in year t.

• Instrument (Z_it) – “shift–share”  
   Z_it  =  (Firm i’s share of 1970 industry j market cap)  ×  (Total market cap of industry j in year t, excluding firm i).  
   – Industry defined at the 2-digit SIC level.  
   – The 1970 share is time-invariant and predetermined.  
   – The time-varying industry‐level shock comes from the summed market cap of all other firms in industry j in year t (“leave-one-out”), purged of firm-specific performance.

• Control (counterfactual)  
   Conceptually, the control condition is the level of CEO pay that would prevail if the firm’s size responded only to idiosyncratic factors net of industry-wide shocks. Empirically, within the 2SLS framework, the residual variation in SIZE_it not explained by the instrument serves as the counterfactual.

• Timing  
   Instrument uses contemporaneous industry shocks, but all CEO-level outcomes are measured in the same fiscal year.  Standard errors clustered at the firm level; robustness to clustering at firm-year two-way by Cameron–Gelbach–Miller.

------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance (Cov(Z_it, SIZE_it) ≠ 0).  
     — Industry boom years meaningfully raise individual firm capitalizations.  Plausible and testable (first-stage F-statistic > 10).

A2. Exclusion (Z_it affects CEO pay only through SIZE_it).  
     — After controlling for year fixed effects and industry linear trends, the sole channel linking aggregate industry shocks to an individual CEO’s pay is via the firm’s own market cap.  Potential violation discussed below.

A3. Independence / Exogeneity (Z_it ⟂ ε_it).  
     — 1970 market-share weights are pre‐period and cannot be chosen in anticipation of future CEO pay shocks.  Industry shocks are driven by macro factors (oil price changes, tech waves, etc.) that CEOs cannot influence.

A4. Monotonicity (no “defiers”):  A positive industry shock weakly increases firm size for all firms.  Plausible given the definition of market cap.

A5. SUTVA: CEO pay in one firm is not directly affected by the instrument of another firm conditional on industry‐year controls.  Reasonable at the firm level, though we return to peer-effects concerns below.

------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Direct peer effects violate exclusion: Industry shocks could raise CEO pay via benchmarking or labor-market competition rather than through own-firm size alone.  
Mitigations  
  • Include industry-year average CEO pay (excluding firm i) as a control.  
  • Re-estimate on subsamples with limited cross-firm benchmarking (utilities, regulated industries).  
  • Use alternative instrument: national market-wide shock × 1970 beta (firm’s historical covariance with market), which is unrelated to peer pay.

T2. Differential trends in industries (technology vs. manufacturing) confound results.  
Mitigations  
  • Saturate regressions with industry × year fixed effects in robustness checks; although this soaks up some power, it directly addresses differential growth trends.  
  • Add industry-specific quadratic time trends.

T3. Measurement error in CEO pay or market cap (e.g., reporting changes post-1992 SEC disclosure rules) attenuates or biases estimates.  
Mitigations  
  • Winsorize pay at the 1/99 percentiles.  
  • Include year dummies; in robustness, drop 1991–1994 transition years.  
  • Compare ExecuComp data to Compustat ExecuComp overlap for consistency.

------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # fast high-dimensional fixed effects & IV
library(modelsummary) # nice tables

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data loading and basic cleaning
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("ceo_compensation_1970_2003.csv")

# Keep required variables & basic filters
dt <- dt[!is.na(ceo_pay) & !is.na(market_cap)]
dt[, `:=`(ln_pay  = log(ceo_pay),
          ln_size = log(market_cap))]

# Industry identifier (2-digit SIC)
dt[, ind2 := substr(sprintf("%04d", sic), 1, 2)]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct the shift–share instrument
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# (a) Compute 1970 industry totals
base_year <- 1970
W <- dt[year == base_year, .(base_cap = sum(market_cap, na.rm = TRUE)), by = ind2]

# (b) Merge base totals
dt <- merge(dt, W, by = "ind2", all.x = TRUE)

# (c) Firm's 1970 share
dt[year == base_year, firm_share := market_cap / base_cap]
dt[, firm_share := max(firm_share, na.rm = TRUE), by = firm_id]   # carry forward

# (d) Year-t industry shock (leave-one-out)
dt[, ind_cap_t := sum(market_cap, na.rm = TRUE) - market_cap, by = .(ind2, year)]

# (e) Instrument
dt[, Z := firm_share * ind_cap_t]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main 2SLS specification
# ln_pay_it = α + β * ln_size_it + γX_it + μ_i + λ_t + ε_it
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
spec_main <- feols(ln_pay ~ 1 | firm_id + year ~ ln_size | Z,
                   data = dt,
                   cluster = ~firm_id)

summary(spec_main)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness: include industry-year peer pay & drop tech industries
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# peer pay control
dt[, peer_ln_pay := mean(ln_pay, na.rm = TRUE) - ln_pay,
   by = .(ind2, year)]

spec_robust <- feols(ln_pay ~ peer_ln_pay | firm_id + year ~ ln_size | Z,
                     data = dt[!(ind2 %in% c("35","73"))],  # drop high-tech
                     cluster = ~firm_id)
summary(spec_robust)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory (Rosen’s superstars; Gabaix & Landier (2008) style scaling) predicts an elasticity of CEO pay to firm size of roughly 1/3.  
Prior: A 10 % exogenous increase in firm market cap will raise CEO total compensation by about 3 %–4 %.  Magnitude may be larger post-1990s when option grants expanded.

------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument relevance (first-stage F-stat > 10)  .............. 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction believable after controls ............. 0.5  
C3: Independence from unobserved CEO shocks ..................... 0.5  
C4: Monotonicity (no defiers) ................................... 1  
C5: SUTVA / stable unit treatment ............................... 0.5  

Total (out of 5) = 3.5.  The two middling scores highlight remaining concerns over peer-benchmarking channels and correlated industry shocks; addressed through robustness checks above.

------------------------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
